What Is Estate Planning Law?

Estate planning law is the process of creating legal documents and asset distribution processes for after a person passes away or is no longer able to communicate. Estate planning documents include a last will, revocable living trust, power of attorney, beneficiary designations, living will, and healthcare proxy. Without estate plans, property transfers go through intestate succession. Individuals use estate laws for probate avoidance, reducing estate tax liability, and protecting inheritance rights. A trustee has a fiduciary duty to carry out trust administration and management.
Speak to an estate planning attorney  to learn how the law applies to your particular set of facts.
Estate Planning Law: What You Need To Know
Your estate is all property owned by you at the time of your death. It can include real estate, life insurance policies, retirement accounts, bank accounts, and personal property.
It’s essential to make sure you have effectively stated your wishes and accounted for all your assets.
A comprehensive estate plan will also designate guardians for your children and representatives to act for you in financial and medical matters if you cannot act for yourself.
The requirements for an effective estate plan vary by state, so it will be vital for you to speak with someone who knows the area’s requirements well.

Your estate is all property owned by you at the time of your death. It can include real estate, life insurance, bank accounts, and personal property, like your car. A comprehensive estate plan can  ensure that your property goes where you want it to go  and that your loved ones can jump through as few legal hoops as possible. You can also designate guardians for your children and representatives to act for you in financial and medical matters if you cannot act for yourself. Many estate plans also include advance medical or healthcare directives through which you can specify the sort of end-of-life treatment you would like to receive.

Will

A will is the way you declare your wishes regarding the distribution of your property when you die. If you die without a will, your assets will be distributed according to your state’s intestate succession laws, and you will not have any control over who benefits from it. The legal requirements for creating a valid will vary by state law, and you may find it beneficial to review your will with a lawyer. There are, however, some general guidelines that you should be aware of.

A valid will is executed by someone with legal capacity and voluntary intent. You will also want to make beneficiary designations that spell out who you want to benefit from the will and what specific property you would like them to receive. The clearer your will, the more likely your wishes will be followed. It would be best if you also considered  naming an executor  or a person who will follow the will’s instructions. If you do not name an executor, the court may appoint one.

You may want to consider adding a guardianship plan setting forth the care of your minor children. This is especially important if you have a specific guardian in mind. In the absence of a guardianship plan, the court will generally appoint a family member as guardian, and, of course, the court does not know your children or your family and friends as well as you do.
Trust

You can create a trust instead of, or in addition to, a will. A trust is an agreement between you and another party called the trustee. The agreement requires the trustee to manage property and assets for a third party, called the beneficiary.

A trust will allow you to maintain control of your assets after your death. For example, you can create a trust to pay for your grandchild’s college tuition, which won’t allow them to use that money for any other purpose. Another benefit of a trust is that you may be able to help your family avoid probate court — the legal process through which estate assets are distributed.  Avoiding probate  will save your family both time and money.

Trust is an umbrella term covering many kinds of trusts, and you may find it beneficial to speak with a lawyer to make sure you pick the right type for your assets. In general, however, you can create a trust that will transfer your property and distribute assets after you die or create one that begins during your lifetime and may continue after your death.
Power of Attorney

Power of attorney  is a written authorization to act for another person. You may want to consider including a durable power of attorney for your healthcare and finances in your estate plan, as it will remain valid even if you become incapacitated.
Finances

Financial power of attorney designates a representative and grants the authority to act on your behalf in financial issues. Requirements vary by state, but generally, the legal document must be signed and notarized.
Health Care

When you create a power of attorney for healthcare (also called a healthcare proxy), you designate a person who will make medical decisions for you in an emergency. This legal document will become effective when a doctor declares that you cannot make medical decisions. Most states require that you be a competent adult when creating the document.

Both types of powers of attorney have a fiduciary duty to represent your best interests. A power of attorney’s authority is typically extinguished by death, revocation, or divorce (if it was granted to your ex-spouse).
Common Questions for an Estate Planning Lawyer
Below are some common questions you might want to consider when meeting with an attorney for legal advice.
Can I change my will?
Can I disinherit my child?
How much do I have to pay in estate taxes?
How much can I give away before being subject to gift taxes?
What is the difference between a will and a trust?
What is the difference between a will and a living will?
Are living wills the same as advance directives?
What type of trust is best for my circumstances?
What happens if I don’t have a will?
What should my estate plan include?
Finding the Right Estate Planning Attorney for Your Needs

It is crucial to approach the right type of attorney — someone who can help you through your entire case. To do so, search the Super Lawyers directory to  find a lawyer specializing in estate planning  near you.
Should I Talk to an Estate Planning Lawyer?

The requirements for an effective estate plan vary by state, so it will be vital for you to speak with someone who knows the area’s requirements well. You may also find it helpful to talk with someone about your assets and your desired outcomes so that you can make sure the plan you create accomplishes your goals.

A lawyer will further anticipate potential problems with your case and advise you on how to approach them. They may even be able to help you avoid potential issues and keep you out of the probate process altogether. Your lawyer will also file all the estate planning documents with the necessary courts and agencies, giving you peace of mind.
